The models also differ in more than conformity: in band rule (at the v1 layer 62, Qwen3.6-27B’s H1 is 0.73; § 5 ), in lens and, for Llama, in prompt format, where the peers’ statements arrive in the user turn. For Qwen3.6-27B and Llama, merely mentioning another bridge, with no flip, lowers the original-bridge readout about as much as giving in (0.50 to 0.19 and 0.52 to 0.20; not for Qwen3.5-4B or Gemma). With four models this is a pattern, not a law. Llama’s result is in line with a study of simulated peer disagreement across four model families in which pressure suppresses the model’s clean-reasoning features ( Kumarappan and Mujoo, 2026 ) . We cannot conclude, however, that Llama keeps no dissent: its readout is also near zero when it is merely instructed to state the peers’ answer (§ 6 ), and with its earlier answer hidden or absent, its agents that gave in read the bridge at 0.25 and 0.39 (§ 4.5 ); within-item ratios do not order the middle models either (§ 5 ). We steered along J-lens directions as in ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) , with our own scaling: we added α ​ ∥ h ℓ ∥ ​ d \alpha\lVert h_{\ell}\rVert d at the last prompt position of one band layer at a time (three evenly spaced band layers; α ∈ { 0 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.8 } \alpha\in\{0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.8\} ), where d d is the unit J-lens direction of an entity: the mean over its probe tokens of J ℓ ⊤ J_{\ell}^{\top} applied to the unembedding row scaled by the final norm’s gain. The outcome is whether the most likely next token is the first token of the original answer; items in which any two of the three answers share a first token are excluded, and shares are pooled over agents and layers (Figure 3 ). The agents are those that gave in during a separate injection run on up to 600 test items (56, 187, 119 and 491 agents). The original answer’s own direction, a positive control, raised the share from at most 4% at α = 0 \alpha=0 to 98%, 89%, 98% and 66%, so the injection works in every model. The original bridge’s direction raised it to 41% [29, 54] (Qwen3.5-4B) and 19% [14, 25] (Qwen3.6-27B) at α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 , against 8% [4, 19] and 9% [5, 14] for a control bridge and 6% and 5% for random directions at the same α \alpha (95% Wilson intervals counting each agent once, although it contributes three layers); at larger α \alpha its effect vanished (0% and 2% at α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 ), while random directions reached 23% and 11%. For Gemma (at most 4%, as for the control bridge) and Llama (0%) it had no effect. These results are exploratory and pick the best α \alpha after the fact; for Qwen3.6-27B the intervals of the original and the control bridge meet. In the Qwen models, pushing the state toward the original bridge can bring back the original answer, so the second hop from that bridge is still usable. In Gemma the bridge is about as readable as in Qwen3.6-27B, yet this intervention had no effect; that does not show that the bridge plays no role, since a push along one lens direction at one position may miss how the model uses it. 4.9. Later rounds and free debate Later rounds (Qwen3.5-4B) Repeating every round verbatim made agents answer “correct” or “identical” by round 3, so a pre-registered addendum, chosen on development data, collapses earlier rounds into one-line moderator summaries. Among agents that gave in at every round, the original bridge was still read in round 3 (R1: 0.54 [0.47, 0.62], n = 49 n{=}49 ), down from 0.86 in round 1 ( − 0.32 -0.32 [ − 0.38 -0.38 , − 0.26 -0.26 ]), and the peers’ bridge remained above the mention baseline (R2: +0.41 [0.29, 0.54]). We did not run later rounds for the other models. Free debate. Three copies of each model debated up to 400 facts (200 known, the others unknown but with the first hop answered correctly) for three rounds; round 0 answers are sampled at temperature 1 and later rounds are greedy. Each agent’s latent vote is the candidate answer (the truth, if some agent stated it in round 0, and the distinct round-0 answers) with the best mean J-lens rank over the band. In round 1 the plurality of stated answers was at least as accurate as the plurality of latent votes in every model (Qwen3.5-4B 0.76 vs. 0.71, Qwen3.6-27B 0.78 vs. 0.70, Gemma 0.81 vs. 0.79, Llama 0.71 vs. 0.69), and so it stayed in rounds 2 and 3 for three models; reading latent answers is thus not a reliable accuracy gain for aggregation. Round-0 votes are not comparable, since all agents share one prompt. Qwen3.6-27B’s stated accuracy then fell to 0.30 and 0.44 while its latent votes stayed at 0.66–0.69. A check with a rule fixed in advance did not attribute this to degenerate answers (8% and 5%). Of the 648 agents right in round 1, 414 switched to an answer no peer had given in round 1 and 2 adopted a peer’s; round-2 answers were often not names (“an island”): the drop is not conformity, but it is unexplained (supplement). Silent dissent in free debate. In an exploratory analysis with rules recorded in advance, we rebuilt each agent’s prompts from the transcripts and read the original bridge in agents that gave in at round 1: right in round 0, then stating a peer’s wrong answer. On known facts only Llama had the 20 such agents we required (29, from 22 facts; 6, 3 and 2 in the other models). They still represented their original bridge (0.20 [0.11, 0.32]; logit lens 0.02; difference 0.18 [0.08, 0.29]), indistinguishable from agents that held against a wrong peer ( − 0.03 -0.03 [ − 0.19 -0.19 , 0.13]) and more than under scripted peers (H1: 0.03), with the earlier answer in view in both, though peers, prompt and which agents give in differ. 5. Robustness Other band rule. For Qwen3.5-4B, the v2 band (23–28) gives H1 = 0.82 and H4 = 0.81. For Qwen3.6-27B, the v1 layer 62 gives a higher H1 (0.73) but no lens difference (H4 = 0.06 [ − 0.01 -0.01 , 0.13]): near the output the logit lens reads the bridge too, which is why rule v2 selects intermediate layers. The other rule selects no layers for Gemma or Llama. Rank threshold. Much of the retained signal lies between ranks 100 and 500: at k = 10 k=10 , H1 is 0.12 for Qwen3.5-4B and 0.00 for the other models; at k = 500 k=500 it is 0.70, 0.41, 0.56 and 0.21, and Gemma’s H4 shrinks to 0.07 (supplement). Clustered intervals and multiple tests. Resampling bridges instead of records widens the intervals (e.g. Qwen3.5-4B’s H1: [0.67, 0.92] from 18 bridges) but leaves 14 of the 15 registered tests with an estimate supported after a Holm correction; the exception is Llama’s H2 ([ − 0.001 -0.001 , 0.056], adjusted p = 0.06 p=0.06 ). These analyses, like the rest of this section, are exploratory; their choices were recorded before they were run. Without a threshold. Comparing the ranks of the original bridge and the control directly, the J-lens ranks the bridge above the control in agents that gave in in every model, by 1.40, 0.48, 0.85 and 0.54 orders of magnitude (bridge-clustered intervals above zero, Llama included). The lens difference persists for Qwen3.5-4B and Llama, vanishes for Qwen3.6-27B and reverses slightly for Gemma ( − 0.07 -0.07 [ − 0.19 -0.19 , − 0.02 -0.02 ]), where the logit lens ranks the bridge above the control as well, but mostly outside the top 100. Same items. Comparing each item with itself, agents that gave in read the original bridge below the same items’ agree readout in every model, and the peers’ bridge above the same items’ mention readout (all intervals above zero; supplement). Peers and lenses. With five peers, H1 is 0.82, 0.24, 0.31 and 0.07. With Neuronpedia’s base-model lens, Gemma’s H1 is weaker but still positive (0.105 [0.065, 0.150]); we report both Gemma readouts because the registered primary lens is the refit. Llama’s refitted lens gives 0.024. On Qwen3.5-4B’s development split, lenses refitted on dialogue, mixed or 100 WikiText sequences change entity readouts by about 0.02 or less. 6. Discussion What is retained. Our readout shows that an agent’s original bridge is still represented at the moment it states the majority’s answer; it does not show that the agent believes it ( Levinstein and Herrmann, 2025 ) . The addendum clarifies what “retention” means here: the bridge need not be carried over from the agent’s earlier statement, since agents that gave in represent it with that statement hidden and when they had never answered; it can be computed again from the question (although in Qwen3.5-4B seeing the earlier answer raises the readout). An agent that yields thus still computes the premise of the correct answer while stating a different one. A development-split control sets a limit. When a coordinator required every agent to state e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} regardless of its belief (compliance about 100%), the original bridge read 0.25 for Qwen3.5-4B and 0.04, 0.01 and 0.00 for the other models, against 0.73, 0.63, 0.79 and 0.48 in round 0, although the first-hop entity and the agent’s earlier answer were in context. An agent told what to say need not compute its own two-hop answer, and then its bridge is not read: a positive reading is informative, a near-zero reading is not evidence that the premise was abandoned. Llama illustrates this: its agents that gave in to scripted peers read almost nothing with their earlier answer in view, but 0.25 with it hidden, and 0.20 in free debate, where it is also in view.
